title: Microelectronics Series 2 Electronic Design Automation and Computational Software Tools 101 1.12.22

cues.text: >> Thank you everyone for joining today's DAU your event.
This is number two of the microelectronics series.
Today we have EDA and Computational Software Tools 101.
My name is Emmett Simmons, I'm the producer for today's event.
The agenda for today, your microphones will be muted.
The session is being recorded.
Please submit all your questions via the chat.
We will verbally respond to your questions towards the end of the event.
There is a survey.
We will be posting the survey link in the chat.
But those who are here for CLPs, the session does qualify for up
to 1.5 CLPs will supervisory approval.
They are not automatic.
You will need to apply for them, but there will be a CLP certificate at the end of the survey
for those who are interested in that.
The recording will be posted to dau.edu/events, which is listed at the bottom.
Now I'm going to turn it over to Dave Pearson to introduce our speakers.
>> Hey, thank you, Emmett.
And thank you everyone for joining us today.
You know microelectronics are critical to all of our modern defense and information systems.
Today to help our Defense Acquisition Workforce get more up to speed on this issue,
we are hosting the second of our four-part series on microelectronics.
If you recall last week, our speakers provided an overview of the series to include discussions
on how microelectronics are designed, manufactured and tested.
Today we're going to continue with the series by covering the development of flow
of semiconductors and the systems they support by discussing electronic design automation
and computational software tools.
We're fortunate again to be joined by two industry leaders in this area.
Mr. James Chu will get us started and he is the chair of the NDIA Science
and Technology Division, and serves as a senior Global Director for aerospace and defense
at Cadence Design Systems, a Silicon Valley-based technology company.
He'll be followed by Frank Schirrmeister, a senior group director for solutions
and ecosystems at Cadence, where he leads a team translating customer challenges
in the hyperscale, communications, consumer automotive, aerospace defense and industrial
and healthcare vertical domains into specific requirements and solutions.
At the end of today's presentation, we should have some time for questions,
so please submit them via the chat box and I'll pass them
on to our speakers once they conclude the remarks.
James, let me pass this over to you.
And thank you for joining us again today.
>> Thank you so very much.
And as I told the crowd earlier, I'm pleased that this time I'm not having
to do it from my neighborhood Starbucks.
Just so you know, I did not get power till the following day.
But that notwithstanding, at least you get to see me in somewhat full dress regalia.
I just want to spend a few minutes to get a level set and maybe give you a little bit
of updates since the last time we last spoke.
I'm going to share my screen.
Hopefully you will all see it.
And then I'll be turning over to my good friend, Frank Schirrmeister in a few minutes.
So let's see if you get this right here and get this right there.
So hopefully can you all see this wonderful picture of my friend Norm Augustine?
It should say why you're here.
Hopefully you can all see that.
So the reason why -- yeah.
Okay. You can all see this, I hope.
>> Yes.
>> Thank you very much.
So this kind of gives a brief summary again to level set.
It really is the department's dependence on microelectronics that continues to give us
that warfighting edge that is really now resulted --
one of the unintended consequences is that we've been using microelectronics
to provide a linear increase in capability with each new platform.
But what's been coming with it has in fact been an exponential cost in terms
of acquisition costs, and probably more important, operation sustainment costs.
For those of you folks who were an operator or know operators,
you know that they have a healthy disdain for new technology, because their job is
to keep all our critical platforms at a certain operational readiness rate.
And introducing something new, and some of them say just for the sake of new,
complicates the operation sustainment and the operational readiness rate
because of the impacts it has on supply chain, and then ultimately in terms
of maintenance, and then the dreaded DMSMS.
Trying to keep certain critical components, critical systems operational
when stuff simply is not made any more and the companies that have them don't make them,
and maybe these systems don't exist anymore.
That has become a critical concern to the department.
You guys have been following Congress, you know how much fun it is to try
to retire platforms they like, such as the A10.
For those of you who -- to give you a little personal background,
when I was in kindergarten growing up near Edwards Air Force Base in the mid-60s,
there was a bomber called the B-52 that was flying over our playground.
Fast-forward that a few years later,
I'm at the Pentagon supporting the Director of Defense Research Engineering.
I'm part of the team that's certifying that airframe to be 100-year-old airframe.
So we keep our stuff around a lot, and the method that we've been using the past
to design systems, which is we have to get it done or else it's curtains for the free world,
while that has maintained our warfighting edge and has made us the mightiest military force
in the world, it does have the consequences of being very expensive to operate and sustain.
So the industry broke this, and this is what we're going to be talking about today.
The industry, the department saw this also and invested in the technology
that my good friend Frank Schirrmeister is going to be talking about,
that created something called electronic design automation.
Now, we talk about microelectronics, but I want you guys
to think about this in an expanded view.
It's not just microelectronics.
This is digital microelectronic engineering, meaning everything is done virtually
and that you know that things will work the way they're designed.
And you do not manufacture, you don't go to fabrication
until you have actually met those goals that you've set for the product.
The other thing that you that you think you'll notice is that within the commercial world,
there is no IOC and then there's an FOC.
There is no beta versions out there anymore.
When the product is ready to release, it's released.
FOC and IOC are exactly the same.
That product is immediately sustainable and monetizable at launch.
And this is all done with the tools
that by my good friend Frank Schirrmeister is going to be talking about.
A little later at the next session, we'll be talking digital twinning, which is really sort
of the core of what Frank will be referring to.
But it really is with this thing about the digital twin, that's where you're able to --
where you hear things such as DevSecOps, and things like that.
And please ask us some questions about that and why you cannot separate hardware
and software development, because that's the other thing that is a unique concept now
that we're introducing to the Department of Defense.
Hardware and software needs to be co-developed such that you will have first pass success
and have that sustainable and maintainable system at launch.
I think the last thing I'd like to mention is
that please don't hesitate to ask us any questions.
There's a lot of stuff on the internet nowadays in terms of emulation
and digital twinning and things like that.
Please take a look at it.
And you know, I think that we would love to have you -- when it comes time for some our companies
and other companies of space happen to have user conferences, I will forward the invitations
to Mr. Pearson and Mr. Simmons, Emmett, when that's available.
They're always free of charge, you're able to attend those and you can see how other users --
how other how the customers of these type of equipment and methodologies we'll be talking
about today, how they're using that to solve their problems.
And then you can talk to a real time expert there.
So with that, I'm going to turn it over to my good friend Frank Schirrmeister
who I think is ready to present a very lively session.
So Frank, over to you, please.
>> Thank you, James.
I will share my screen here from my side.
Doing this, so you should be able to see the screen now.
So this will be the second out of the four-part series session.
Last week I stood in for Paul McClellan who was out sick that day
for the first session on Semiconductor 101.
Today I will dig one level deeper and double click into the computational software tools
and electronic design automation that enable these chip developments.
For those of you who haven't seen me last week, the accent is German.
I graduated from the University in Berlin, did a lot of software development myself
to finance my university, did several chips at the time for motion estimation and audio
and running MPEG for video processing.
And then came in 97 to Silicon Valley.
I have enough sense, there's a lot of good sunshine, a lot of cool companies here,
have done participation in several books over the time.
And if you want to connect on LinkedIn and follow my blogging,
the links are up in the upper right here.
So with that, let's dig into the intended learnings for today.
This is really about an intro, what's in a system of systems?
So I'll tear down an F-35 a little bit.
I will talk about how EDA and technical software, electronic design automation,
fits into the supply chain, how a generic flow looks like
and then how the development tools top to bottom look like.
How do hardware and software mechanics actually work together?
I'll double click into the generic design flow we introduced last week, and then go into how
to get from an idea to the integrated chips in boards
and packages where the effort is spent today.
How FPGA is fitting into all this, how hardware and software are interacting a little bit.
And then as a brief double click into one of the three main domains, verification,
ensuring functional correctness, digital implementation --
that's where you have automation to get
from a high level description into implementation of a chip.
And then custom implementation, which is manual implementation, which is used a lot
for highly specialized circuit and analog mixed signal chips.
And then I'll talk about system analysis.
So that's the next level up from a perspective of how these chips are then integrated
and how the systems fit together.
Let's dig into it.
As an introduction, what's in a system of systems really here?
I don't have an F-35 in my backyard, sadly.
But I have this information here from online information about how many parts.
It's amazing, it's arguably probably one
of the most complex systems we have, systems of systems.
It was 200,000 parts, 1,600 suppliers, 200 distinct chips,
3,500 other circuits, lots of software.
And that's only the main tool, okay?
Each of the subcomponents has its own chips underneath.
You have all these different systems and all these different components in here with respect
to things like the vehicle system itself.
You have very advanced display components, communications,
navigation, identification, so forth.
Very complex system of systems.
And I mean systems of systems.
And this is just to point this out, this is conceptual.
I didn't really look into an F-35 design in that amount of detail.
I just said there will be communication somewhere.
And I used an example communication system here with some information just to make the point,
you basically have subcomponents here which are systems,
the kind of RX you would have in the plane.
But there might be other x like in data centers or somewhere else.
And at the source of it, you have these chips that run lots of software in parallel.
So those are the semiconductor-based components.
So it's a complex design chain.
And what we are now talking about is the tools that are needed to build these
and what the development flows are for those.
So here's a generic design flow.
Somebody on a napkin designed an F-35.
That's actually a real picture I found online on a site.
And then you want at the end of the system of system coming out of it.
So the generic design flow is really a flow of designing,
partitioning and refining your system.
And this is having three levels here.
There may be more levels, but at the end, you have parts you develop
in software, electronics and mechanics.
So you have these different components here developed, and then you have integration,
verification and validation of these items in the integration phase
when you integrate everything together.
Well, if you'd make no mistakes up here, during this phase, it says no misunderstandings
between different interfaces and so forth.
Well then all will go perfectly here.
Reality is, of course, slightly different.
Mistakes are just part of life.
So what we call intelligent system design, where here in our domain, electronic design
and computational software, we really need to consider software, hardware,
mechanical effects all of them together, as well as analog and digital.
And the idea of the tools we are talking about is always to bring these integration aspects
into an earlier phase of the design flow.
Instead of building it and integrating it, figuring out it doesn't work,
do a virtual integration early on.
And that's what often is referred to as digital engineering, bringing hardware and software,
different components together, even different domains
like the electromagnetic bits, and do early integration of it.
So that's the generic design flow.
And why are we doing this and where does this set of tools and everything, all this fit in?
Well, let's go back to the world economy.
I thought that's fun, given that we are all talking about economy and everything.
In 2019, the world economy, the GDP was about close to $88 trillion.
So that says on it up to $90 trillion.
You see there's an interesting chart here on howmuch.net,
and I used some of the World Bank data afterwards.
So if you look into this, and start with the global GDP and break this down, where we fit in,
industrial is about a third of it.
So the rest is services up here.
Then the systems and OEM components --
so the systems we are building like the systems I mentioned earlier, with respect to the boxes
that have electronics in it -- that market was about $2.4 trillion.
The semiconductor market enabling this is about $429 billion.
And then just to put myself and EDA into its place, technical software was about $51 billion.
But it's enabling all these markets here at the end, enabling us all together.
And if you now zoom into these components here and put in the domain you are interested in,
the aerospace defense domain here, that's part of this domain, which is expected to grow
to about $2.9 trillion in 2025, according to some estimates.
And the semiconductor market is expected to grow to $534 billion.
And then the tools market I'm talking about here today is expected to grow to about $80 billion,
and the semiconductor bit is here in this EDA field.
So that's about $12 billion.
And then you have simulation and analysis for computational software.
Here you have some of the mechanical CAD aspects,
here you have product lifecycle management in here.
So it's a rather big chunk here enabling the overall industry.
That's where semiconductor design EDA fits in.
So how do we get there?
I mean, we have our napkin and we want to go down here.
This is the LDR breakdown from a while back.
You may have seen this.
You have your system, you design and refine it into different components underneath.
You have a large slew of suppliers here.
And you deal with really defining what are your components, hardware, software, mechanics?
You have then different ways of implementing from here.
You can do custom off the shelf.
You have potentially field programmable areas, FPGAs.
You can do custom silicon.
So you have a large number of potential implementation options for your design.
And as you have the subsystems which you then need to integrate,
even in a case of custom off the shelf tooling with hardware and software,
you use a lot of tools for system modeling.
So UML SysML to develop software on cards.
And then even if you then buy components and build it, you have system integration tools
that allow you to integrate all those.
So you need to take the components, put them into boards, and then integrate them from here.
If you choose underneath to go to a more custom implementation
and do custom chip implementation further down, then you really need
to not only do the tools you do in any case, like packaging
and computation fluid dynamic tools, you also then need for custom silicon
to build the chips underneath where you would reuse some building blocks
from existing libraries.
So that's kind of like object-oriented design for hardware.
So you reuse components, like for example vision, digital signal blocks.
You verify that everything works together.
You then do digital and custom implementation of the chips,
and then you check that everything is correct.
And after you put it into packages and PCBs,
and then do system analysis, putting it all together.
So that's kind of like the broad stroke flow of how everything fits together.
And I already had mentioned the virtual integration.
A lot of the things you do here, you actually model items early
with a digital twin model early on.
We have a special section on that, as I think the third or fourth component of this series.
Bringing these actual implementations, digitalizing them
and having virtual integration early on.
So now let's talk about the development steps for semiconductor.
Last week, we had this canonical flow here which had pointed out the different steps
from a high-level description and system VeriLock.
So here you have a -- that's a textual description.
Using synthesis into a netlist.
So a netlist is at the circuit level,
the gate level implementation of these textual description.
And then from here, we're doing the physical design, which creates the layout.
And that layout is then given to physical verification, and afterwards it's given
to the fabrication, the semiconductor fab to implement all this,
to really put these onto a set of masks.
And then these masks are used to create in complex steps the actual silicon as it runs.
So to give you an analogy how this works, one of the things I've prepared is a video
which you can also look at yourself offline.
So that video is actually just on YouTube.
And I'll play that for you as an overview.
[ Music ]
>> Without Cadence, there would be no cell phone, no GPS,
no internet, no drones, no self-driving cars.
Okay, maybe self-driving cars aren't real yet, but they will be,
thanks to designers using Cadence tools and IP.
Designing a new system is much like designing a house.
First, you need an architect to come up with a basic floor plan.
Then you need another expert to do the electrical plan,
and yet another one for the plumbing.
Oh, and what about custom cabinets in the kitchen?
Yet another expert is needed to custom design that.
It turns out that designing something like your cell phone is not
that different than designing a house.
Designers start with floor plans for all of the electrical parts that go into it
and end up with chips instead of a house.
Imagine if instead of meeting up with a plumber, the electrician,
and many others to update the plans for your house, you could just click a button
and it would all happen automatically.
That's what we're trying to do at Cadence.
We have all the tools to automate the steps from a chip idea to something
that is used to make the electronic product.
Not everything needs to be designed from scratch though.
Just like some of the cabinets in your house were bought at the hardware store,
at Cadence we have many off the shelf parts that chip designers can use just as they are.
But just like you customized your kitchen, we can also make it easy
for designers to create something special.
That's what we call the Cadence implementation flows.
I'll bet you've been frustrated by things in your home
that weren't done right the first time.
For that kind of issue, we have what we call verification tools.
They make sure that the design will create a chip that works just
like the building inspectors do for home designs.
These tools check the things like electrical wiring that's not accidentally interfering
with the plumbing and that everything fits together.
These days, full neighborhoods are planned with houses, retail, restaurants
and recreation areas that all fit together nicely.
In the cell phone design, the equivalent is connecting all these chips together
on what are called circuit boards.
All these chips are interconnected and Cadence tools make sure they work together well.
Cadence is the only company that can cover all parts of the electronic design process,
from idea to silicon and systems.
We are the one stop shop.
And we are ready as every day brings new challenges.
To illustrate how much things are changing, the San Francisco Bay Area grew from 4 million
to about 8 million people over the last 40 years, roughly by 2x.
Well, the number of items that we deal with in a chip grew by a factor of 50,000
over the same time, and it's only getting more complicated.
This data traffic is huge.
You know how you're always trying to get more bandwidth
on your internet connection to stream movies?
Yeah, that's only going to get more challenging.
Our economy runs on this data now, and Cadence is enabling all the developments around it
that make it better for everyone.
This is why Cadence customers are bringing innovative technology
to you to make your life better.
>> Okay, let me close this one, get rid of this.
So this is kind of meant as an analogy of how our tools enable these chips,
just like you would build a house more in layman's terms.
So let's dig into this in more detail and give you first an appreciation of the complexity.
So the video showed a little bit about that, about the 50,000x improvement.
This is really what we had last week discussed as Moore's law,
where the number of transistors increases every year.
This is a Locke scale here, right?
So this is doubling every 18 months.
And they have different definitions.
But you see this curve of the transistors here.
One of the things which happened over the last two decades really is
that we had this multicore revolution, if you will,
where you have multiple cores necessary to do the compute.
And that is because with just single-core scaling, we were running into power issues.
You would have had power issues and the thread performance --
basically the computer architecture didn't give you the improvements anymore,
which was pointed out by a gentleman named Herb Sutter with The Free Lunch is Over.
There's another couple of key publications, which if you want to do some research
on your own, Moore's law here in the late '70s.
And then for software, there was this discussion about there is no silver bullet,
which is this notion of how complexity in software grows.
And then most recently, a couple of years back, Professor Hennessy and Patterson talking
about the new golden age of semiconductor design.
And to give you some timeline components in here, Linux was coming in here in the '90s
and Android later here, and that was somewhere between --
I think 2007 is the first point here I put into this chart.
So the complexity of these devices has grown, given that this is a Locke chart
at just unimaginably large pace and complexity.
And the impact of what we do in EDA and technical software is nicely shown here.
In the ITS roadmap in 2001, they said --
ITRS is International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors --
they said, the cost of design is the greatest threat
to continuation of the semiconductor roadmap.
So that's really the key challenge, cost of design.
And famously, I was said that a cost of a system on chip that in 2011 was about $40 million.
Without the improvements we would have done for hardware and software improvements in EDA
from 1993 to 2009, the same chip would have cost about $7.7 billion to design.
So what we do with this EDA is really every couple of years, roughly every decade,
we move up in the level of abstraction at which we do design.
And then EDA does the automation of this.
So we do model at a higher level of abstraction, verify here where it's faster,
and then implement and automate with EDA the implementation.
That has been great for really the last five, six decades, if you will.
What has happened now recently is this thing we had talked about as Moore's Law has slowed down.
So we are no longer getting this free lunch, if you will,
of improvements by adding more transistors.
And then for big designs, servers and CPUs,
we actually have approached now what we call the vertical limit of semiconductors.
Vertical, when you look at the chip wafer we had pointed out last week, vertical the piece
which steps over the wafer, step by step.
And that's really from a perspective of optical and implementation perspective,
the limit to which you can really design those.
And now the design size approaches the radical limit.
And what has happened there really now from here, we are going into this phase --
and that's what John Hennessy and David Patterson pointed out --
of much more domain-specific architectures and domain-specific languages,
which require you to disaggregate the classic SOC and do heterogeneous integration.
What we mean by that is, instead of doing simply bigger chips in two dimensions,
we are replacing this with 3D IC with 3D integration.
So we use a third dimension, which gives us shorter wires, better power, better performance,
better bandwidth between the different components.
We can make it smaller, and better yield because we no longer
for big designs are designing at the vertical limit.
It's not easy to do that, though.
You need to carefully plan this, you need to deal
with implementation, thermal effects, power effects.
You need to have multiple chips, multiple die as we call them
that are integrated within a package.
You need to have that timing signed off together,
have to verify them together and then test them.
So it's a whole slew of new challenges.
And we are now coming to this point where we had for a long time already its systems and package,
they are really now becoming co-packaged chips where everything is integrated with several die,
several semiconductor components are integrated within a package.
So that's what we refer to as heterogeneous integration with multichiplet packaging.
That's a big next step in automation which we are tackling.
So taking a step back, going back to our design flow, and go from the simple canonical flow,
what we have done here is we have developed these EDA tools to verify first the design
at the gate level and the verilog level.
We have tools to implement automatically, from here to here.
So that's what we call synthesis tools.
And then we have also tools that do custom layout where you build custom implementation.
So going back to the house analogy from earlier on where you have the custom cabinets
in the kitchen, and some of them we use.
So that's what the custom implementation do for chip design.
And that's required for analog and mixed signal and RF circuitry, for sure.
And then, on top of what this canonical flow that we introduced last week provides,
you also have a lot of reuse of existing building blocks.
So you really don't start with a blank sheet.
You reuse subsystems, you use processor cores, you reuse peripherals.
And then, of course on top of this, you will have to deal with a lot of software
that runs a lot of the functionality on top of the hardware.
So now let's double click into this flow and look into this flow in a timeline.
This sounds all very nice.
You just describe something, you call up some tools and they implement it for you.
In a timeline perspective, it is looking as follows.
So you have elapsed time for the flow,
you have some hardware building blocks that you may reuse.
And then you have, for new blocks you do manual development of those blocks.
This is really what we call RTL, register transfer level.
Where you then with a process we call functional verification are reducing the number
of defects over time.
So that's happening.
And this can be a process which, as James pointed out, referring to some of the consumer
and server chip designs, this is often then having a timeline like Christmas you need
to have it ready for production back here.
So you need to work back from there.
Those timelines can be 12, 18 months, sometimes for chips,
but you'll always have specific timelines you need to meet.
Once you have enough verification done,
you do the physical design and the digital or custom way.
You get this GDS II tape out we talked about last year.
You cross your fingers while everything is in fabrication, that's 18 months.
You get your silicone back integrated into a PCB or into a package, the 3D IC.
And then that's getting you these -- that has the different steps overlaid here now,
basically having the manual RTL, having reuse of IP, getting this to the layout level.
And then from here, running the verification in parallel.
For the digital fill flow I had showed earlier, these are the symbols I used earlier.
And then you have the 3D IC and packaging integration here for the design.
So now you have a board, one of those PCB boards or a package chip.
And going back to your idea earlier on, verification really never finishes.
You get this down -- you try to get this down to as little defects remaining as possible.
But you continue verifying throughout the cycle.
If you now take this component, which is just a chip and the board and put it in perspective,
you really also have to take into account hardware and software.
The IP blocks you have reused early on, you need to verify them all together
in this step called functional verification.
And from a system level perspective, before you actually have started your chip,
you actually have reused some functional building blocks,
and hopefully you have done some system model, because if you haven't,
you find at the integration phase as we showed in the three diagram earlier,
you have at the integration phase for sure lots of bugs to deal with.
So with system modeling I mentioned UML and sysML earlier,
and hardware and software partitioning.
You have hardware and software partitioned together, partitioned out with the hardware flow
down here and the software flow up here.
The software, if you dig now into details
from for this component, the software also uses reuse.
So a lot of the blocks you will license and buy.
You will port an existing real time operating system.
You compile, link and debug your software creating these components of software
from drivers through the operating system, middleware and applications.
And then you run them at different phases in this process we call verification and hardware,
software co-optimization using different tools throughout the process.
And I'll double click into those tools in another hot minute here.
So from here, the dynamic hardware/software verification that happens pre-silicon, right,
so you have all these things already happened in the timeline well before you even have taped
out the chip, and well before you have your actual silicon design back.
So this can be about 18 months' time for some of the more complex chips.
Having done all this, you now integrate it all into your product, into your board.
And you can from here build this into your systems of systems.
And remember, this was only one
of the components underneath in my F-35 break down early on.
So there's early hardware/software integration on emulation and prototyping,
what James often refers to as integrate and emulate before you fabricate.
That allows you to do software development typically off those levels middleware
to firmware early on.
We typically don't develop like the full application like an Angry Birds
or your Word application before the silicon is available,
but we abstract some of those items away.
So that's the conceptual flow.
This has become very complex, I build it over the last five minutes.
If you now look into the effort estimates for this, so this is the same timeline we had here,
the same timeline below with the fabrication, the post-silicon validation.
If you look at the percentage of effort up here, this is from data we have done
with International Business Systems, IBS.
If you look into the effort, the big chunks are to qualify which IP you're using.
The verification is very, very time consuming -- a lot of effort, a lot of resources.
And then the implementation, the digital implementation
from that to layout is very important.
More than half of the effort, though, is actually spent on software development.
And this application software development,
here we mean the software that directly runs on the chip.
So having said that, hardware and software have very big components
in the overall project chair.
So this is again data from IBS, separating mature and advanced designs,
where for advanced designs at smaller technology nodes, you see here, the software aspects
in green, the hardware aspects in blue.
And this is verification, this is implementation.
So they can be very significant.
One of the things, you see the numbers here --
so this is $350 million for a project here in seven nanometer and so forth.
That sounds very, very significant.
It is very significant.
You will need lots of return from a project like this.
